content: Sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) is defined as the sudden and unexpected death of an infant under one year of age, with the fatal event typically occurring during sleep. This diagnosis is made when the cause of death remains unexplained after a comprehensive investigation, which includes a complete autopsy, an evaluation of the circumstances surrounding the death, and a review of the infant's clinical history. Despite the implementation of various prevention campaigns, SIDS continues to be one of the leading causes of infant mortality. In 1994, researchers proposed the triple risk model to explain SIDS. According to this model, SIDS occurs when three factors converge: (1) the infant has an underlying vulnerability, (2) the infant is in a critical developmental period for homeostatic control (which is age-dependent), and (3) the infant is exposed to an external stressor. Since the early 1990s, epidemiological studies have suggested an association between the use of pacifiers (also known as dummies) and a reduced risk of SIDS. If pacifier use is proven effective in reducing SIDS through randomized controlled trials, it could serve as a cost-effective preventive measure due to its low cost. The objective of this review was to determine whether the use of pacifiers during sleep, compared to not using pacifiers during sleep, reduces the risk of SIDS. To address this question, the authors employed the standard search strategy of the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group. They searched multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE via PubMed, Embase, and CINAHL, up to March 16, 2016. Additionally, they reviewed clinical trial registries, conference proceedings, and reference lists of relevant articles to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomized trials. The inclusion criteria for the review were as follows: controlled trials (both published and unpublished) that used random or quasi-random allocation of infants. Eligible participants included infants born at term, preterm (less than 37 weeks of gestation), or with low birth weight (less than 2500 grams). Infants had to be randomized by one month of postmenstrual age. The authors also planned to include studies reported only in abstract form, as well as cluster and cross-over randomized trials. Two independent reviewers assessed the studies identified through the search. However, no eligible randomized controlled trials were found that examined the use of pacifiers for reducing the risk of SIDS. In conclusion, the authors found no evidence from randomized controlled trials to either support or refute the use of pacifiers as a preventive measure for SIDS.
